New Jersey UI Reemployment Demonstration
T2: JSA+Training/Relocation vs T1: JSA-only

Anderson, Corson & Decker 1990, NJ UI Reemployment Demonstration Follow-up Report, Tables II.4 (p.21) and II.5 (p.22); T2-T1 contrast derived from T-vs-C impacts and SEs assuming equal outcome variance and independent treatment samples.

Q1 post-claim; impact of adding training/relocation services to JSA-only (T2 minus T1). Impact in pp; control_mean = T1 (JSA-only) employment rate. Derived: T2-C 0.015(0.013); T1-C 0.018(0.014); N_T1=2416, N_T2=3810.

Q2 post-claim; impact of adding training/relocation services to JSA-only (T2 minus T1). Impact in pp; control_mean = T1 (JSA-only) employment rate. Derived: T2-C 0.002(0.012); T1-C 0.021(0.014); N_T1=2416, N_T2=3810.

Q3 post-claim; impact of adding training/relocation services to JSA-only (T2 minus T1). Impact in pp; control_mean = T1 (JSA-only) employment rate. Derived: T2-C 0.005(0.012); T1-C 0.012(0.014); N_T1=2416, N_T2=3810.

Earnings impacts (all time frames) extracted from Couch 1992 Table 1, which uses SSA earnings records matched to NSW participants — 8 years of postprogram follow-up in 1978 dollars. Couch covers AFDC women and youth target groups only (ex-addict/ex-offender records were omitted from the SSA tape provided). ST=1979 single-year, MT=1980 single-year (Couch flags 1980-1981 for potential SSA data quality issues), LT=mean of 1982-1986 yearly impacts (Couch's framing of the sustained long-term effect window; all five years sig at p<0.05 or p<0.10). Employment impacts left at MDRC 1980 values (months 10-18 and 19-27) — Couch reports earnings only. NSW enrollment spread across 1975-1979 (median ~1977), so calendar years map approximately to post-RA years; cadence columns document the calendar windows. Significance in Couch Table 1: * = 5%, ** = 10% (reversed from usual convention).

Earnings are self-reported, calculated as hourly wage × hours/week × weeks/month. All dollar values in 2006 dollars. Report groups outcomes into two 4-year blocks (Years 1-4 and Years 5-8) rather than single years. Years 1-4 (center ~Year 2.5 post-HS graduation) assigned to medium-term; Years 5-8 (center ~Year 6.5) to long-term. The 8-year overall average is $174/month ($2,088/year, 11% over control). Employment impacts reported as months employed rather than employment rate; not entered. SEs not reported in exhibits; only significance stars provided (*** = p<0.01). Technical Resources companion (Kemple and Willner 2008) would contain SEs but is not in our collection. Full-time, one-year program for young adults 18-24: six months of classroom training in IT and financial services occupations, business communication, and professional skills ('Learning and Development'), followed by six-month internships at major companies. Includes weekly stipends, behavior contracts, social worker support, and post-graduation job placement assistance. (Fein and Dastrup 2022, pp.3-4)

Schochet, Burghardt, and McConnell 2008 (American Economic Review 98(5)), 'Does Job Corps Work? Impact Findings from the National Job Corps Study.' Table 4 (p.1875) Annual Social Security Earnings Records (SER) column for LT impacts (calendar years 1997-1999 = Years 3-5 per the report's timing convention, 1995 $). Baseline info from Table 1.

SER (Social Security Administration Summary Earnings Records) cover all workers with a Social Security number. Preferred administrative data source because it has full national coverage (unlike UI which covers only 22 states). Calendar year earnings and employment from Table 4 (p.1875). Time horizons: randomization midpoint ~mid-1995; CY1997 ≈ Year 2 → short-term (Year 1 has lock-in effect from program participation), CY1998 ≈ Year 3 → medium-term, CY2003 ≈ Year 8 → long-term. Employment measure: fraction with nonzero SER earnings in calendar year (ppt). Earnings impacts were positive and significant in 1997-1998 but faded completely by 1999. Authors emphasize this as their key finding: gains not sustained (p.1876). 77% lacked HS diploma/GED at baseline (Table 1). Cost: $16,500 per participant (p.1883), in 1995 dollars. Stars: * p<0.10 (two-tailed), but the paper's Table 4 marks significance at the 0.05 level with * — need to verify. Table 4 note says '* = Statistically significant at the .05 level, two-tailed test'. Mean age not reported as a single number; 75% were ages 16-19 (Table 1). UI data available for only 22 states (subset); not used as separate row because of limited coverage. V13 UPDATE: All impact estimates updated to Schochet (2020) W-2/IRS tax data. Earnings in 2015 dollars. Employment: fraction with W-2 form in calendar year (pp). LT impact switched from Schochet 2020 calendar-year-2003 (Year 8) single-year to Schochet, Burghardt & McConnell 2008 SSA-based Years 3-5 average (calendar years 1997-1999, 1995 dollars). Per-year SSA earnings impacts: Y3 (1997) +$173* (SE 85), Y4 (1998) +$218* (SE 103), Y5 (1999) +$33 (SE 118); pooled SE = RMS of yearly SEs. lt_followup_years = 4 (midpoint of Y3-Y5). Per-year SSA employment impacts: Y3 +0.8 pp (control 76.9), Y4 +2.4* pp (control 78.9), Y5 +1.5* pp (control 83.0). lt_emp_se left blank for binomial computation at analysis time. Note: Table 4's only sig threshold is * = 5% two-tailed, so '*' in source maps to '**' in our convention; Y3 and Y4 SSA earnings were 5% sig individually but the Y3-5 average is n.s.

Schochet 2020, Long-run labor market effects of the Job Corps program--Evidence from a nationally representative experiment.pdf; Schochet, Burghardt, and McConnell 2008, Does Job Corps Work--Impact findings from the National Job Corps Study.pdf

McConnell and Glazerman 2001, Table VII.1 (p.151). Also: reduced other programs $2,186, reduced crime $1,240. Total gross social benefit = $30,957. Net social benefit = $16,829 ($2.02 per dollar). Pooled across all three JOBS demonstration-entry cohorts (1989, 1990, 1991). The report does NOT publish a cross-cohort aggregate; impacts and demographics pooled here. Impact pooling: weighted mean of cohort impacts using total impact-sample size (N_T+N_C) as weights (1989 N=9,174; 1990 N=5,989; 1991 N=11,726; total N=26,889). Demographic pooling: weighted mean using CRIS-E sample sizes from Exhibit 2.1 (1989 N=8,485; 1990 N=4,674; 1991 N=12,976). Standard errors: back-solved from significance stars where present (* → /1.645, ** → /1.96, *** → /2.576); for n.s. impacts, derived by scaling a starred sibling cohort's SE through sigma = SE / sqrt(1/N_T + 1/N_C). Pooled SE = RMS of cohort SEs (sqrt(mean(SE^2))) per analysis convention, conservative for downstream random-effects meta-analysis where between-study variance dominates. lt_earn SE left blank: no starred anchor for any LT outcome — couldn't pin sigma. National Supported Work: MDRC-designed federal demonstration providing subsidized employment in generic work crews. Not a CBO in the Peck sense (MDRC was the national contractor). No sector-specific employer engagement, no staffing agency partnerships, no dedicated job development beyond the subsidized employment itself.

public: NSW was funded by a consortium of federal agencies (DOL, HEW, HUD, LEAA) with early support from the Ford Foundation. By the time of the full demonstration, federal funding was dominant. Ford Foundation's role was primarily catalytic (creating MDRC and seeding the project). Operational funding for the work sites was overwhelmingly public.

private: MDRC (a nonprofit created by Ford Foundation) coordinated the demonstration nationally. Local operators were community-based organizations and nonprofits that ran the supported work sites. Government agencies funded but did not directly administer the program.
AFDC group: avg 9.5 months in supported work positions. MDRC 1980, Table 2-7, p.36.

program_uptake uses attendance rates (% of scheduled hours worked) from Table 2-7, 'Key Operational Performance Indicators by Target Group,' doc p.36, PDF p.54. These are attendance rates among those offered the program, not enrollment rates per se. Control group was not offered Supported Work positions (control_mean=0). The 18-month embargo on controls accessing SW is described on doc p.19.

NSW is subsidized transitional employment, not classroom training or job training in the traditional sense. 'Any training from any source' rates are not reported. Table 4-5 (AFDC only, doc p.66, PDF p.84) reports CETA/WIN/government job participation but this captures subsidized employment, not training. Left blank.

Primary: JTPA Title II-A is a job training program. The three main service strategies are classroom training in occupational skills (41% of adult women, 24% of adult men), OJT/JSA (31% of women, 44% of men), and other services including basic education and work experience. Training/classroom instruction is the core purpose of Title II-A.

has_classroom=1: 24-41% of participants assigned to classroom training in occupational skills. has_ojt=1: OJT component for 31-44%. has_jsa=1: JSA bundled with OJT track. has_multiple_components=1: most participants received a combination. other_components: basic education, GED prep, work experience available as 'other services' track.

Primary: JOBSTART's core components are basic education (GED prep) and occupational training. The program is explicitly modeled on Job Corps to provide classroom education and vocational training to school dropouts. Job placement is a secondary component.

has_classroom=1: all sites provide basic education and/or occupational training as core. has_ojt=0: JOBSTART does not include on-the-job training or paid work experience (explicitly excluded due to JTPA constraints, p. ES-3). has_jsa=1: job placement assistance is one of four core components. has_multiple_components=1: four core components (education, vocational training, support services, job placement). other_components: support services including child care and transportation (Table 3.3).

Secondary: GAIN is fundamentally a mandatory welfare-to-work program, not a training program. Basic education/classroom instruction is one pathway (for those scoring below minimum on literacy/math tests), but the other pathway is immediate job search. Riverside, the highest-impact county, explicitly emphasized employment-focused services over education. Training is a component, not the core service.

has_classroom=1: basic education, GED prep, ESL for registrants determined 'in need'. has_ojt=0: no structured OJT component. has_jsa=1: job search activities for those 'not in need' of basic education; Riverside emphasized job search for all. has_multiple_components=1: combines mandatory participation, basic education, job search, and sanctions.

FIRST-STAGE FLAGS: (2) C crossover rate of 3.4% includes 20 members who joined Year Up after the 3-year embargo ended; during-embargo crossover was only 9/871 ≈ 1.0%. Paper uses 3.4% and does not adjust for crossover. (3) any_training measures credential receipt from any source (Exhibit 3-2), not training participation per se. A person could train without earning a credential, or earn a credential from prior training. 70.1 - 54.4 = 15.7 but exhibit reports 15.6 (rounding). Implementation report (Fein and Hamadyk 2018) may have more direct service receipt data.

mixed: Year Up's operating revenue comes from a combination of employer fees for interns (~50%), private philanthropy, and government grants. No single sector dominates.
private: Year Up is a national nonprofit organization that directly operates its programs.
Year Up: 6 months classroom training + 6 months corporate internship = 12 months total. Juras et al. 2022; PACE Year Up report.

T enrollment: 96% (p.9 text: 'Staff encouraged treatment group members to enroll in Year Up (96 percent did so)'). C crossover: 3.4% (footnote 40, p.4: '29 cases represent a very small fraction — 3.4 percent — of the entire control group'; 9 admitted during embargo + 20 after embargo ended). Impact = 96.0 - 3.4 = 92.6 pp. N uses full randomization sample (1,668 T + 871 C from Exhibit 1-1).

Exhibit 3-2, 'From various sources (6-year survey)' section, row 'Any source', p.32. T=70.1%, C=54.4%, Impact=+15.6 pp, SE=2.7, p<.001. NOTE: This measures receipt of a credential (from a college, another education/training provider, or a licensing/certification body) — not training participation per se. program_uptake_impact=56: Exec Summary p. viii: '56 percent of the treatment group had enrolled in occupational training, an increase from 48 percent in the first 18 months.' Section 3.3, p. 24: '8 percent of the treatment group enrolled in occupational training for the first time after the short-term follow-up' (48+8=56 by 3 years). Exhibit 3-1 note, p. 23: 'Almost 62 percent of treatment group members (375 of 609) enrolled in any training within 18 months' — the 62% includes College Readiness bridge participants who had not yet progressed to occupational training. Using 56% (occupational training enrollment by 3 years) as program_uptake. program_uptake_control_mean=0: C barred from Pathways to Healthcare by design (see Exec Summary footnote 4, p. vii).

SSA earnings records (SER)

Primary: Job Corps IS a training program. Its core services are academic education (GED prep, basic education) and vocational training. Residential setting and support services are facilitating infrastructure, not the intervention itself.

has_classroom=1: academic education (GED prep, basic education) and vocational courses. has_ojt=1: vocational training includes hands-on occupational training components. has_jsa=0: no formal job search assistance component described. has_multiple_components=1: classroom + vocational training + residential services + counseling + health care.

Sample sizes: Table 4, bottom row, N = 9,264 treatment + 5,874 control (p.1875). Demographics: Table 1 (p.1867): 59% male, 27% white, 48% Black, 18% Hispanic, 77% no HS credential. Randomization period: p.1865 ('November 1994 through February 1996'). Cost: p.1883 ('about $16,500 per participant'). Follow-up rate: SER has near-complete coverage (administrative records).

ST (CY1997): Table 4, 'SER Data' panel, row '1997', 'Earnings Impact' column = 173 (SE 85); 'Fraction with Earnings Impact' column = 2.1 (SE 0.6). p.1875. MT (CY1998): same panel, row '1998', Earnings Impact = 218 (SE 103); Fraction with Earnings = 1.3 (SE 0.6). LT (CY2003): same panel, row '2003', Earnings Impact = -9 (SE 178); Fraction with Earnings = 0.2 (SE 0.6).
ITT regression-adjusted impact, estimated via OLS with controls for baseline demographic characteristics. Table 4 note: 'Regressions control for sample member characteristics.' (p.1875)

Randomization Nov 1994 – Feb 1996, midpoint ~mid-1995. CY1997 ≈ Year 2 post-RA → short-term. Year 1 (CY1996) would be preferred for ST but shows heavy lock-in effect (treatment group in program), so Year 2 is the first clean post-program year. CY1998 ≈ Year 3 → medium-term. CY2003 ≈ Year 8 → long-term (latest available year in Table 4, well within 3+ year window).
SEs reported directly in Table 4, in parentheses below each impact estimate.
p.1883 text: 'about $16,500 per participant.' In 1995 dollars. Gross cost, not net.

McConnell & Glazerman 2001: $16,489/'participant' is per actual Job Corps enrollee (TOT). Confirmed by (a) the national-program benchmark of ~$1B for ~60,000 annual enrollees ≈ $16,667/enrollee, (b) the cost-benefit ratio formula on p. 180 ('percentage gain from participation' = ITT impact / counterfactual outcome of participants, i.e., TOT scaling), and (c) the report's consistent use of 'participant' to mean someone actually enrolled in Job Corps (~73% of program group). WARNING: the earnings impact estimates in the row are ITT (per program-group member). To compare cost and benefit on a like-for-like basis, either scale impacts by 1/0.73 (TOT) or scale cost by 0.73 (per program-group member ~ $12,037).

FLAG: Significance notation — Table 4 uses * = p<0.05 (two-tailed), NOT * = p<0.10. This differs from most other studies in the extraction. I have recorded stars based on the SEs and t-stats: |173/85| = 2.04 → ** (significant at 0.05), |218/103| = 2.12 → ** (significant at 0.05), |2.1/0.6| = 3.5 → *** (significant at 0.01), |1.3/0.6| = 2.17 → ** (significant at 0.05). FLAG: Short-term is Year 2 not Year 1 because Year 1 has program lock-in. FLAG: Earnings gains fade completely after 1998 — this is the paper's central finding. FLAG: Cost is gross, not net (no estimate of control group service costs). FLAG: 73% treatment take-up rate means ITT attenuates effects. FLAG: Control group embargoed from Job Corps for 3 years (ended ~1999); long-term estimates are post-embargo.

National Job Corps Study: Federally-funded residential training program (admin=public). No CBO lead, no employer engagement in curriculum design, no staffing agency partnerships, no formal employer hiring commitments.
public: Job Corps is 100% federally funded through annual DOL appropriations (~$1.7B/year). No private operational funding.

mixed: The Office of Job Corps within DOL designs the program, sets standards, and provides oversight, but individual Job Corps centers are operated by private contractors (for-profit companies like MTC, Management & Training Corporation; and nonprofits). Day-to-day program delivery is by private entities under federal contract. Changed from 'public' to 'mixed' upon review.
Average stay in Job Corps ~8 months. Schochet et al. 2008.

program_uptake: Schochet, Burghardt, and McConnell 2008, p.1871: 'About 73 percent enrolled in centers' (treatment group). p.1868: 'only 1.4 percent of controls enrolled in Job Corps before the end of their three-year embargo period.' Footnote 2, p.1869: 'An additional 3.2 percent of control group members enrolled in Job Corps after their three-year restriction period ended.' Control total = 1.4 + 3.2 = 4.6%. Impact = 73.0 - 4.6 = 68.4 pp.

Text p.1871 confirms: 'About 93 percent of treatments enrolled in education and training programs' and 'About 70 percent of controls enrolled in education and training programs other than Job Corps.'

ITT derived from Bloom-adjusted TOT. Original estimates from Bell & Orr 1994 Table 2 / Bell et al. 1987 Table III.3 are per training entrant (TOT via Bloom 1984 adjustment). Converted to ITT by multiplying by state-specific entry rate (0.91), derived from Bell et al. 1987 Table III.1 per-assigned/per-entrant ratio. ITT = TOT × entry_rate; SE(ITT) = SE(TOT) × entry_rate. Significance levels unchanged (t-stats preserved under Bloom).

Post-demonstration year 2: demonstration period ~6-11 months, post-demo year 1 = next 12 months, post-demo year 2 = remaining months through ~33 months after enrollment. Midpoint of post-demo year 2 ≈ 27 months ≈ 2.25 years → medium-term per CKW classification (1-2 years boundary; 2.25 years closer to medium center 1.5 than long center 4+).

SE originally reported in Bell & Orr 1994 Table 2 (in parentheses below coefficient) as TOT (per training entrant). Converted to ITT SE by multiplying by entry rate (0.91): SE(ITT) = SE(TOT) × entry_rate. Per Bloom (1984), t-statistics are identical for ITT and TOT.

Treatment 2: JSA Plus Training/Relocation

Training role = 'secondary'. The Treatment 2 intervention was JSA plus an offer of training or relocation through JTPA. JSA (orientation, assessment, service plan) was the primary component delivered to ALL Treatment 2 members; training was an additional option with very low take-up: only 299/3,810 (7.9%) received training per tracking system, ~15% per JTPA records. Only 7 received relocation assistance. The text explicitly states (p.289) that 'the additional offer of training did not have a positive impact on employment and earnings' and that impacts were generally smaller for Treatment 2 than Treatment 1 (JSA only). However, training IS part of the Treatment 2 package, making it eligible for inclusion. Training component = secondary, JSA = primary.

Secondary. The pooled experimental group includes three models: Model I (work experience only, ~1/3 of sample), Model II (education/vocational training, ~1/3), and Model III (mixed work+training, ~1/3). Formal classroom training is the primary component of Models II and III (~2/3 of experimentals), but only counseling (Adkins Life Skills, VITAS) was provided in Model I. Since the RCT comparison pools all three models vs. control, training is not the sole or primary component for the full treated group.

has_classroom=1: Model II provides GED prep, ESL, vocational courses (woodworking, welding, word processing). has_ojt=1: Model I provides structured work experience (renovation, painting, landscaping) with supervision. has_jsa=1: All models include job placement assistance, Adkins Life Skills Training (job search skills), VITAS vocational counseling. has_multiple_components=1: Program bundles work experience, training, counseling, and placement. Training_role='secondary': Options was a comprehensive welfare-to-work program. While it offered GED prep, basic literacy, and vocational training, these were part of a broader menu including job search, work experience, and ongoing case management. The program's primary goal was self-sufficiency through any employment pathway, not specifically through classroom training. About 19% of experimentals participated in education/training vs. 25% in job search and 17% in work experience (Table 4.1, p. 62).

has_classroom=1: GED prep, basic literacy, vocational skills training offered (Ch. 1, p. ix). has_ojt=1: On-the-job training with private firms, partly financed through diverted welfare grants (Ch. 1, p. ix). has_jsa=1: Group and individual job search were core components (Ch. 1, p. ix; Table 4.1). has_multiple_components=1: Program bundled job search, work experience, education/training, OJT. other_components: Unpaid work experience (workfare) for up to 13 weeks was a major component.

Training_role='secondary': SWP was a comprehensive mandatory welfare-to-work program. Participants were assigned to one of three streams: job search, CWEP (work experience), or education/training. Education/training was one of three streams, not the primary intervention. The program's core feature was mandatory participation and saturation coverage of the caseload, with emphasis on work requirements and job search. User confirmed training is a small component. (Ch. I, pp. 1-5; Ch. II, pp. 16-23)

has_classroom=1: Education and training stream included GED prep, basic education, and vocational training (Ch. II, pp. 20-21). has_ojt=0: No structured OJT or apprenticeship component described. II, pp. 18-19). has_multiple_components=1: Three streams (job search, CWEP, education/training) plus assessment and sanctioning. other_components: CWEP (Community Work Experience Program) = structured unpaid work in public/nonprofit agencies for up to 13 weeks.

Simple difference in means (PSWP group vs. control group), no regression adjustment. Tables V-A through V-D report raw means and differences. Table IV reports pooled differences with p-values from t-tests. Our ST/MT values are N-weighted averages of the cohort-specific raw differences.

ST: QTR+4 = 4th quarter after random assignment ≈ 12 months. All 4 cohorts have data through QTR+4, making this the most robust short-term estimate. st_followup_years=1.0. MT: QTR+7 = 7th quarter after RA ≈ 21 months. Only Cohort A (enrolled Jan-Mar 1986) has data this far out. mt_followup_years=1.75. This is the longest available follow-up from this interim report. Placed in MT bin as it approaches the ~2-year horizon. No LT data: interim report covers at most 7 post-RA quarters.

Employment SEs: Not estimated (per user instruction). Earnings SEs: Imputed via sigma-backout method. Step 1: From pooled Table IV, QTR+4 earnings diff=$42.25, p=0.0448. z = Phi^{-1}(1 - 0.0448/2) = 2.007. SE_pooled = 42.25/2.007 = $21.05. Step 2: Back out common sigma: SE² = sigma²(1/N_T + 1/N_C). sigma = SE_pooled / sqrt(1/4462 + 1/3751) = 21.05 / 0.0000222^0.5... Actually: 1/4462 + 1/3751 = 0.000491. sqrt = 0.02215. sigma = 21.05/0.02215 = $950.3. Step 3: Per-cohort SEs: SE_i = 950.3 * sqrt(1/N_Ti + 1/N_Ci). A: 37.9, B: 43.9, C: 42.7, D: 47.0. Step 4: Combined SE_avg = sqrt(sum(w_i² * SE_i²)) where w_i = N_Ti / sum(N_T). ST (4 cohorts): SE = $21.5, t = 42.25/21.5 = 1.97 → ** (5% level). MT (Cohort A only): SE = $37.9, t = 42.56/37.9 = 1.12 → not significant. Cross-check: Cohort C imputed SE=42.7, diff at QTR+4=$135.95, t=3.19. Table V-C reports p=0.0015 for this cell; Phi^{-1}(1-0.0015/2)=3.17. Consistent.

1. COHORT AVERAGING: Impacts are N-weighted averages of 4 cohort-specific results, not from pooled Table IV. This creates an unbalanced panel (4 cohorts at QTR+4, only Cohort A at QTR+7). The pooled table restricts all cohorts to 4 common quarters. 2. MT FROM ONE COHORT: QTR+7 uses Cohort A only (N=1712/990), so MT is less precise and may not generalize across cohorts. 3. NO REGRESSION ADJUSTMENT: Raw mean differences, no covariate controls. 4. INTERIM REPORT: Only 12-month follow-up for Cohort A, less for others. A final report with 24-month data was planned for April 1989. 5. SAMPLE SIZE DISCREPANCY: Table II pooled N (4539/3828) does not equal sum of cohort Ns (4539/3674). Control total discrepancy of 154. Per-cohort Ns from Tables V-A through V-D used for impact calculations. 6. SMALL EMPLOYMENT EFFECTS: ST employment impact of +1.48pp is small and would not be statistically significant even if SE were computed. 7. NO FIRST-STAGE DATA: T vs C service receipt comparison deferred to final report. 8. CWEP AS MAIN COMPONENT: Despite education/training stream, CWEP (workfare) and job search appear to be the dominant activities. Training role correctly coded as secondary. 9. ADVERSARIAL REVIEW CORRECTION: Cohort B and D treatment/control Ns were initially swapped in the weighting computation. Corrected values verified against Table IV pooled totals (4462/3751). Corrected ST earnings impact ($42.25) matches Table IV exactly. TAKEUP_AUDIT: Hogarth, Martin, and Nazar 1988 interim report participation data not located — may be in later impact report.

Training_role='secondary': Ohio JOBS was a mandatory welfare-to-work program with assessment-driven activity assignments. CWEP (community work experience) was the single most common assignment (47% of ever-assigned, 19.1% of all treatment). Basic and post-secondary education together comprised 49% of ever-assigned (20% of all treatment). Job search activities (job club, job readiness) were also prominent. Training/education was a major but not exclusive component. The program was designed around mandatory participation requirements and caseworker-directed placements, not specifically around classroom training. (Exhibit 2.3, p. 33)

has_classroom=1: Basic education (12% of all T, 30% of ever-assigned) and post-secondary education (7.7% of all T, 19%) are formal classroom instruction. has_ojt=0: CWEP is unpaid work experience in public/nonprofit agencies, not employer-based OJT with training objective. No structured OJT described. has_jsa=1: Job club (9% of all T, 22% of ever-assigned) and job readiness training (4.7%, 12%) are job search assistance activities. has_multiple_components=1: Bundles education, job search, and work experience.

1. EMPLOYMENT MEASURE: 'Percent Ever Employed' during each year = fraction with any UI-recorded earnings in any quarter of the year. Not a point-in-time rate. This may overstate employment relative to quarterly rate measures used in other studies. 2. LOW PARTICIPATION: Only 40.5% of treatment group ever assigned to any JOBS activity over 3 years. The ITT impact is diluted by non-participation. 3. 9:1 RANDOMIZATION: Unusual ratio (9 treatment : 1 control). Small control group (N=1,314) reduces precision relative to a balanced design with the same total N. 4. CONTROL GROUP CONTAMINATION: 12% of original controls received JOBS services; these were removed and remaining controls reweighted (footnote 18, p. 13). 5. NEGATIVE EARNINGS FOR 1990 COHORT: The 1990 cohort showed significant negative earnings impacts (-$319** Year 1, -$482** Year 2), attributed to opportunity costs of E&T participation for clients with stronger labor force attachment (Exhibit 3.3, p. 56). 6. MEAN AGE NOT AVAILABLE: Only categorical distribution reported. 7. RACE: Only white/non-white breakdown available; non-white=23.5%. 8. PROGRAM START-UP: Random assignment began at program start-up (Jan 1989), capturing early implementation period unlike CA GAIN or FL PI which waited ~1 year. Cohort heterogeneity substantial (esp. 1990's negative earnings vs. 1989's positive). User accepted pooling: within-experiment cohort variation < between-experiment variation in the downstream random-effects meta-analysis.

1. QUARTERLY cadence: impacts and control means are per quarter, not annual. 2. Largest effects of any pathway — employment +15.1pp, earnings +$1,740/q — remarkably large for a ~2-month training program. Worth flagging for plausibility. 3. Demographics not reported by pathway. 4. Cost per treated ($7,509) is program-wide, not pathway-specific. 5. Small sample (51 T, 52 C) but highly significant results (p<0.01). 6. Strong for patient access cohort; unclear for medical billing/coding. For the 4 Goodwill medical billing/coding cohorts, no specific evidence of employer input into curriculum. Overall employer partnership described as 'loosely coupled' (p. 54).
